items.title: Abroad, Spain’s Leader Is a Left-Wing Hero. Will He Lose Power at Home?
items.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a staunch critic of President Trump, faces an uphill task to overcome a right-wing challenge in the national election on Sunday.
items.full_text:
Title: Abroad, Spain’s Leader Is a Left-Wing Hero. Will He Lose Power at Home? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/europe/spain-pedro-sanchez-conservatives-election.html

Published Time: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 05:15:54 GMT

Markdown Content:
In his eight years as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez has gained international renown among left-wing voters for his welcoming [position toward migrants](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/16/world/europe/spain-amnesty-immigration.html), his [pivot to renewable energy](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/20/world/europe/spain-iran-energy-renewables-gas-sun.html) and his criticisms of big tech companies, the [Israeli government and President Trump](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/04/world/europe/trump-spain-iran-sanchez.html), all as the Spanish economy boomed.

That reputation may count for little in Spain’s national elections on Sunday, which are essentially a referendum on Mr. Sánchez and which seem likely to remove him from power. Polls have consistently forecast that he will be replaced by a coalition of the mainstream conservative People’s Party and a far-right ally, Vox. That would mark the return of far-right nationalists to the Spanish government for the first time since the Franco dictatorship ended in 1975.

With [far-right parties also gaining strength](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/05/world/europe/europe-far-right.html) ahead of major elections next year in France, Italy and Poland, the elections in Spain amount to the latest barometer of the continent’s willingness to let long marginalized forces back into power. Though nationalist leaders have lost recently lost power in [Hungary and Serbia](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/world/europe/serbia-hungary-elections-trump.html), they are surging in France, where Marine Le Pen [leads all rivals](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/08/world/europe/marine-le-pen-presidential-campaign.html); in Germany, where the far right is set to [lead a state government](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/world/europe/germany-afd-saxony-anhalt.html) for the first time since the defeat of Nazism; and now in Spain.

“Having post-fascist formations, either as the leading force in their countries or inside the government, is a mortal wound, a very hard blow, to the postwar European philosophy,” said Guillermo Fernández-Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University of Madrid. He added that a loss by Mr. Sánchez would mean that “supporters of the European project are becoming fewer and fewer.”

Vox has campaigned on a platform of expelling illegal migrants, reducing benefits for legal ones and scaling back the European Union’s involvement in Spanish affairs.

Image

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, speaking last weekend in eastern Spain.Credit...Eva Manez/Reuters

Image

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the People’s Party, this month in Bilbao, in northern Spain.Credit...Ander Gillenea/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

If Mr. Sánchez manages to pull off a victory, it would amount to yet another stunning turnaround for perhaps Europe’s most accomplished political survivor. He came to power [against the odds in 2018](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/03/world/europe/spain-pedro-sanchez.html) and kept it over three elections, [including one](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/16/world/europe/spain-pedro-sanchez-government.html) in 2023 that few thought he had a shot of surviving.

“With all the things that we have passed over the last years,” Mr. Sánchez said in an interview on the campaign trail, “I think that I have made a positive impact in my society, in my country and in Europe.”

He explicitly predicated his campaign on holding back Europe’s right-wing wave. He argued that he would continue on a left-leaning path, pursuing multilateral international relations and a robust welfare system, which he has fortified by increasing pensions and creating a minimum basic income.

The last days of the campaign seemed like a handout frenzy, as he raised minimum wages and salaries for government workers, and extended time off for bereavement.

Those pledges, and his skill on the campaign trail, have helped him gain steam leading up to the election, in which Spanish voters elect 350 members of Parliament. A candidate needs the support of a majority of lawmakers to govern and often needs help from smaller parties to cross that threshold.

Mr. Sánchez’s Socialist Party has risen in the polls by drawing support from weakened leftist parties, but that could make it harder for him to form a winning alliance.

Image

A campaign rally for Mr. Sánchez on Tuesday in Barcelona. He has explicitly predicated his campaign on holding back Europe’s right-wing wave. Credit...Josep Lago/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Now, after tacking left, Mr. Sánchez has sought to win over a small but decisive group of moderate voters by promoting a moderate economist to the position of vice premier, by embracing the Spanish flag that was long a symbol of conservatives and by assuming a measured, almost subdued and stately manner in debates.

Still, some moderates have expressed frustration with Mr. Sánchez’s divisive depiction of the right as Franco’s political descendants, just as they balk at the harsh language and anti-migrant sentiment of the hard right.

“He’s trying to win back the voters he lost by moving leftward,” said Cristina Monge,a political scientist and the author of “Against Discontent,” a book about growing disaffection with democracy. She added, though, that many voters seemed especially partisan in “the most ideological campaign I have ever experienced.”

Mr. Sánchez has a lot else going against him. He has faced [corruption scandals](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/22/world/europe/spain-abalos-sentenced-corruption-sanchez.html) in his inner circle, a national [electricity blackout](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/28/world/europe/spain-portugal-power-outage-what-we-know.html) last year, a [migration crisis](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/01/world/europe/spain-ceuta-migrants-morocco.html) this summer, [spiraling rents](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/world/europe/spain-eviction-sanchez.html) and two horrific [train crashes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/world/europe/spain-train-crash-rescue-victims.html) this year.

“A leader who has been in power for eight years suffers from wear and tear,” said Luis Cornago-Bonal, a researcher and political scientist at the London School of Economics.

Under Mr. Sánchez, Spain’s unemployment rate has fallen, its gross domestic product has grown and its deficit has shrunk. Last year, Spain accounted for more than 40 percent of the jobs created in the European Union.

But Mr. Cornago-Bonal said that although Spain’s macroeconomic picture had improved, “voters haven’t always felt that improvement.”

And even for those who had, he said, the strength of an it’s-the-economy-stupid message was diluted in a fragmented and highly polarized Spain.

Image

A protest against evictions and high rent prices last month in Barcelona.Credit...Manaure Quintero/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

For years, conservatives have chanted, “Pedro Sánchez, son of a bitch,” essentially wherever they gather, including in soccer stadiums and on street corners. In the days before the election, Mr. Sánchez said, his daughters heard it at a disco.

The animus against Mr. Sánchez surged [after the 2023 election](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/16/world/europe/spain-pedro-sanchez-government.html). Then, the People’s Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who is again its candidate and the country’s most likely next leader, won more votes than Mr. Sánchez, but not enough to win outright.

Vox had underperformed, and together, it and the Popular Party did not win enough seats to form a government. Mr. Sánchez then cobbled a minority government together, with the support of small parties from Catalonia that want independence from Spain.

To win their backing, he [pledged amnesty deals](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/30/world/europe/spain-catalonia-independence-amnesty.html) for separatists convicted of leading [a 2017 push for Catalan secession](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/26/world/europe/spain-catalonia-referendum.html) — breaking his promise never to make such concessions, which are anathema to the nationalist right and to a segment of his own Socialist Party voters.

The about-face kept right-wing voters mobilized for years.

Some political analysts blame Vox’s ascension partly on Mr. Sánchez. For years, he focused on Vox as a boogeyman to mobilize his own left-wing voters, but in the process, he bolstered the far-right party’s profile.

“He has been a driver of polarization because his only viable argument was always fear of the far right,” said Daniel Gascón, a political columnist for the newspaper El País. “He has extensively shined the spotlight on Vox.”

Image

Campaign posters for Spain’s main political parties this month in Bilbao.Credit...Vincent West/Reuters

Officials in Mr. Sánchez’s government privately acknowledge that they sought to scare supporters to the ballot box, but argued that they did so because Vox was scary.

Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, wants to deport all undocumented migrants and strip benefits from legal migrants to give more to Spanish citizens.

The party says the European Union is too intrusive in Spain’s affairs, has called for laws repealing some abortion rights and wants to cut funding to feminist organizations that support victims of gender violence, arguing that those groups are partisan and absorb resources that should go directly to victims. In Vox’s view, feminism has gone well beyond equal rights for men and women, and has become oppressive to men.

Vox is against gay marriage and has opposed Pride parades in city centers, though it supports civil partnerships and says it opposes discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Referring to the

items.title: Far-Right Vigilantes Have Inflamed France’s Unrest, Officials Say
items.summary: Through weeks of antigovernment unrest, hard-right activists have fought with left-wing counterparts in at least 10 towns, according to national and regional leaders.
items.full_text:
Title: Far-Right Vigilantes Have Inflamed France’s Unrest, Officials Say - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/europe/france-right-gangs-unrest.html

Published Time: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 05:23:10 GMT

Markdown Content:
One afternoon last month, two groups faced off in a street of Rouen, a city in western France. At one end, men shouted far-right chants and held flags appropriated by right-wing extremists. At the other end, masked demonstrators held a banner with a left-wing slogan.

“I feel like a war is about to break out right in front of me,” said Ulysse Thevenon, a French freelance journalist, as he [filmed the scene](https://www.tiktok.com/@ulyssethevenon/video/7697681742420806944). The footage showed that the two groups eventually clashed, throwing punches and hurling projectiles, but it did not depict how the clash started.

That violent scene on Oct. 17 went largely unnoticed, on a day when mass demonstrations across the country mutated into [widespread arson and looting](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/world/europe/france-protest-riots-marseille.html) in Paris and other cities. The day’s unrest was a turning point in France’s autumn of discontent, which was expected to continue on Saturday with more antigovernment protests planned across the country.

Initially, the centrist government and conservative leaders largely blamed far-left activists for that national unrest.

Now, prosecutors and officials are increasingly pointing to a more complex reality, one that is illustrated by the standoff in Rouen.

Far-right activists have exacerbated the unrest in at least 10 French cities, often clashing with left-wing activists under the guise of repelling looters, according to the national government and officials in those cities. The police arrested far-right activists in at least three cities, leading to the trial of at least 10 people accused of conspiring to commit violence.

In two cities, witnesses and left-wing politicians have accused the police of collaborating with the far-right activists. Footage of some of the clashes, verified by The New York Times, appeared to show police officers shielding masked civilians who were fighting with antigovernment demonstrators. The police and the interior ministry did not respond to requests for comment, but the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has publicly denied collaboration between police officers and far-right activists.

Image

Masked protesters amid clashes in Paris in October.Credit...Pedro Nunes/Reuters

President Emmanuel Macron, in [a broadcast interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xRIw-ZmDzj4), acknowledged the role of the far right in the unrest. “Whether it comes from the ultraleft or the ultraright, those who commit acts of violence against property or people must be arrested, because public order must prevail,” Mr. Macron said last month. Though he rejected accusations of police collaboration, he said that “full light must be shed on these events.”

A spokesman for one of France’s main ultraright groups, [Union and Defense of the Young](https://www.instagram.com/udj.officiel/), said his group never fought protesters unless they were attacked first — and denied working with the police.

In France, extreme-right activist groups engaged in street violence are labeled “ultraright” to distinguish them from far-right political parties. Those include the National Rally party of Marine Le Pen, the front-runner in next year’s presidential election, whom some ultraright activists consider too moderate. She undertook a decade-long effort to soften the image of her National Rally party, though many of its candidates in a recent legislative election were found to have made [racist and antisemitic remarks](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/11/world/europe/france-far-right-bardella-national-rally.html).

Over the past decade, the government has cracked down on the most prominent ultraright nationalist cells, banning several. Still active despite those bans, the groups collectively have roughly 3,500 members, who generally believe that immigration and Islam are a threat to French and European culture, according to Jean-Yves Camus, an expert on the far right at the Fondation Jean Jaurès, a left-leaning think tank.

Those groups have been involved in occasional dramatic confrontations. In 2023, up to 100 of them descended with iron bars and baseball bats on a city where [a 16-year-old white teenager](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/07/world/europe/france-stabbing-romans-sur-isere.html) had been killed, saying it was an anti-white murder; 13 were later convicted of participating in the violence, according to news reports. In February, a [young far-right activist](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/18/world/europe/france-beating-activist-far-left-right.html) died after a fight with a far-left group.

The clashes in October were “not the first time that far-right groups have mobilized in the context of social movements,” said Sébastien Bourdon, the author of [a book](https://www.seuil.com/ouvrage/drapeau-noir-jeunesses-blanches-sebastien-bourdon/9782021566284) on far-right activism.

“What we witnessed this past October was distinct for its scale,” he added.

During the autumn unrest, about 100 “masked ultraright activists” in Nice appeared in the center of that city to “physically confront demonstrators,” injuring three people, according to the city’s prefect, or top local official. Ten people accused of involvement in the episode stood trial this week and are awaiting judgment.

Image

Vandalizing a tourism office in Lyon in October.Credit...Jeff Pachoud/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

In Brest, activists did Nazi salutes in front of a war memorial, according to the city’s mayor. In Lyon, a group “insidiously mingled” with a demonstration in support of shop owners “in an attempt to co-opt it,” the local prefect announced [on social media](https://x.com/prefetrhone/status/2112480200655032493?a=iFVEHJoHc1cQQYhqiYo&s=20). He also [filed](https://x.com/prefetrhone/status/2112567769975718322?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E2112567769975718322%7Ctwgr%5E99a73d6306d498e9940eeef14ddb92c57ae0678a%7Ctwcon%5Es1_c10&ref_url=https%3A%2F%2Fworkflowy.com%2F) a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, accusing the activists of making “Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.”

In Montpellier, videos of a clash on Oct. 24 between antigovernment demonstrators and vigilantes drew concerns from witnesses and left-wing politicians that the police had collaborated with the vigilantes.

The footage, filmed by a freelance photographer, David Hutin, shows a fight between antigovernment demonstrators and men who generally wore white armbands that marked them out as vigilantes.

The footage showed police officers allowing the vigilantes to shelter behind their lines. It also showed the police detaining one of the vigilante’s opponents, while doing nothing to stop one of the vigilantes from kicking the detained man as he lay on the ground.

Accusations of police collusion were further fueled by comments on a public Telegram group used by vigilante organizers in Montpellier.

On the day of the confrontation, one of the group’s administrators said in a public voice note: “There was cooperation and coordination with the police every time — communication that went smoothly.”

The group’s administrators, who declined to comment, did not identify themselves as far-right activists and called on the vigilantes to fight only if provoked. But in messages reviewed by The New York Times, other members of the group called for the vigilantes to attack without provocation and used racist language to describe the anti-government demonstrators. One asked if the activists should “stone” Black people and people of North African descent — using a racial slur to designate the latter.

Image

French riot police personnel during demonstrations in Paris in October.Credit...Ed Jones/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Prosecutors in Nancy are also investigating the police’s handling of clashes between far-right and far-left groups there, following more accusations of police collaboration.

The spokesman for the ultraright [Union and Defense of the Young](https://www.instagram.com/udj.officiel/) — who asked to be named only as Lucien to avoid legal repercussions — described his group, founded in the city of Lyon, as nationalist and revolutionary.

He said its members adhered to the idea of the “[great replacement](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/15/world/europe/france-elections-pecresse-great-replacement.html),” a racist conspiracy theory that falsely maintains that the West’s white populations are being intentionally replaced by nonwhite immigrants. He said they were also anticapitalists, opposed to neoliberal economics and consumerism.

He said that the group defended shops during recent unrest, but declined to say whether it clashed with demonstrators affiliated with the far left.

But according to the interior ministry, the primary aim of the ultraright activists was not to protect shop owners.

“While they claimed their mission was to protect businesses, in reality, they more frequently sought out confrontations with far-left activists,” the ministry said in a statement.

James McManagan contributed reporting from London, and Giulia Imbert from Paris.

items.title: FIFA May Scrap the Peace Prize It Gave to Trump
items.summary: Gianni Infantino, the global soccer body’s leader, has stirred concern over his ties to President Trump. Now FIFA is rethinking the award he gave Mr. Trump last year.
items.full_text:
Title: FIFA May Scrap the Peace Prize It Gave to Trump - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/europe/fifa-peace-prize-trump-infantino.html

Published Time: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 05:18:31 GMT

Markdown Content:
Last December, Gianni Infantino, the president of FIFA, handed President Trump the global soccer body’s inaugural peace prize. Mr. Trump may be the last to receive the award.

FIFA recently [assigned a committee](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7695724/2026/10/16/fifa-peace-prize-scrapped-donald-trump/) to review why the prize was created and whether it should even exist. The soccer body is leaning toward canceling or rebranding the award, according to three senior soccer officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal deliberations.

The push to rethink the prize reflects broad concern over the close ties between Mr. Infantino and Mr. Trump, as well as questions about who would accept any subsequent prize, two of the senior soccer officials said.

FIFA declined to comment beyond repeating that a decision would be made “in due course.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Over the past year, the FIFA Peace Prize has become one symbol of Mr. Infantino’s rocky tenure at the top of global soccer, particularly his effort to [court the U.S. president](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/05/us/politics/trump-fifa-peace-prize-world-cup-infantino.html).

Mr. Infantino created the award in 2025 after [a Venezuelan activist](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2025/10/10/world/nobel-peace-prize) was awarded that year’s Nobel Peace Prize. He presented the FIFA version at the World Cup draw that December to Mr. Trump, who called it “one of the great honors of my life.”

The 2026 World Cup was dogged by questions about political interference, particularly after FIFA lifted the suspension of a U.S. player after [a phone call](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/05/us/politics/trump-fifa-balogun-world-cup.html) between Mr. Infantino and Mr. Trump.

Not long after, it emerged that Mr. Infantino had held secret talks to sell a part of future tournaments to a private fund run by the brother of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. That plan drew outrage and prompted investigations and calls for Mr. Infantino to resign.

Mr. Infantino has denied wrongdoing and has been crisscrossing the globe on a Qatari private jet to [shore up support](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7790138/2026/11/18/fifa-infantino-ffe-election-uefa/) ahead of his re-election bid in March. Shelving the prize would be a concession to his critics.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian soccer federation, said, “The prize awarded at the draw in Washington, D.C., last December lacked legitimacy and any basis in FIFA’s statutes and bylaws.”

In the prelude to the World Cup, Mr. Infantino appeared focused on wooing Mr. Trump. Mr. Infantino relocated to the United States two years before the tournament and aligned himself closely with the American president, acting as a booster for him at public events, traveling on foreign trips with him and [signing a $4 million lease](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/world/europe/fifa-trump-tower-infantino.html) for an office at Trump Tower that largely sits empty.

The creation of the peace prize was rushed and secretive, with functionaries given only weeks to organize it, the senior soccer officials said.

FIFA had considered hosting the World Cup draw ceremony in Las Vegas but opted instead for Washington, in part because holding the event there was [more likely to guarantee Mr. Trump’s attendance](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/09/world/europe/world-cup-infantino-trump.html).

A trophy for the soccer peace prize was commissioned from a pair of Azerbaijani sculptors, one of whom had a son serving as a FIFA official.

The December ceremony featured Mr. Infantino bestowing Mr. Trump with a golden medal, a certificate and the trophy.

“This is what we want from a leader: a leader that cares about the people,” Mr. Infantino said at the time. “We want to live in a safe world, in a safe environment.”

Mr. Infantino’s Trump ties have also drawn the attention of congressional Democrats. In July, Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, opened an investigation into the links. In a letter seeking documents about the relationship, Mr. Raskin described the peace prize as a “hilariously fake” and “bogus” attempt to flatter Mr. Trump.

FIFA said in a statement that discussions had been held with the House Judiciary Committee. “We look forward to addressing any of their remaining questions,” FIFA added.

Some FIFA officials expressed frustration about the creation of the peace award, according to the senior officials and others familiar with internal discussions. That anger deepened as Mr. Infantino’s Trump ties put the organization under increased scrutiny.European soccer’s governing body, UEFA, cited the peace prize in a letter sent to FIFA last month demanding answers about the relationship.

On Oct. 15, FIFA asked the governing body’s social responsibility committee to assess the merits of the peace prize. The committee is led by Zaw Zaw, the president of the Myanmar soccer federation, who is a businessman who was on U.S. sanctions lists over his alleged support for the military junta in his country. He did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Infantino [remains the front-runner](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7483997/2026/09/06/gianni-infantino-future-fifa-president-2027-election/) to win another four-year term leading FIFA, largely because he is backed by the heads of most national soccer federations. Many of those federations rely on FIFA for much of their funding.

One possibility for the soccer peace prize is that the award is reshaped into something presented to figures who have contributed to the sport, the three senior officials said.

A decision could come on Dec. 15, when FIFA’s governing council holds a meeting in Qatar.

items.title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is His Plaque at Denny’s
items.summary: The chain said it had restored a plaque honoring Mr. Huang above a booth in San Jose, Calif., where he is said to have developed the idea for Nvidia.
items.full_text:
Title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is His Plaque at Denny’s - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/business/dennys-jensen-huang-nvidia-plaque.html

Published Time: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:31:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
[America’s diner](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/02/business/media/02adco.html) is always open, especially for Jensen Huang.

Denny’s, the restaurant chain, has reaffirmed its ties to Mr. Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, days after he was [reinstated as the company’s chief executive](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/nvidia-jensen-huang.html).

“Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s,” Denny’s [posted on its social media accounts](https://x.com/DennysDiner/status/2125714117864366416?a=RjxsNFEWruoyB8SadYk&s=20) on Wednesday, alluding to Mr. Huang’s path from washing dishes at a Denny’s as a teenager to becoming one of the most powerful figures in artificial intelligence and one of the world’s richest people.

Legend has it that Mr. Huang developed the idea for Nvidia in a booth at a Denny’s in San Jose, Calif., in 1993 with his co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. In 2023, the restaurant put a plaque above that booth commemorating Nvidia’s beginnings, inviting Mr. Huang to unveil it.

Two weeks ago, Mr. Huang [resigned as chief executive](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/technology/nvidia-jensen-huang.html?eafs_enabled=false) of the chip maker after revelations that he’d had extramarital affairs with an executive who reported to him and with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese spy.

The day after his resignation, Denny’s wrote in its post on Wednesday, the company learned that the commemorative plaque had come down.

“We put the plaque right back up where it belongs,” it said.

Denny’s did not say when the plaque was restored — and multiple calls to the San Jose location on Thursday morning went unanswered — but its statement came two days after Nvidia’s board of directors [reinstalled Mr. Huang](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/business/nvidia-jensen-huang.html) following pressure from President Trump.

Mr. Huang’s comeback has been met with mixed reactions. Some [congressional Republicans have harshly criticized](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/technology/republicans-trump-jensen-huang-nvidia.html) Nvidia’s decision to reinstate him and argued that the Trump administration had not provided adequate assurances that it had resolved national security concerns surrounding the company. Mr. Huang’s allies, including in the tech sector, have supported him, with Elon Musk comparing his exit to “[kicking Michael Jordan off your team](https://x.com/dealbook/status/2123188895986733367).”

Denny’s, too, offered its unequivocal support for Mr. Huang. “We couldn’t be prouder of the history we share,” it wrote.

The company’s statement was met with bafflement on X, where one user said it “might actually be one of the cringiest things I’ve ever seen on this website.”

If such allegiance to another company’s executive seems out of the ordinary, Mr. Huang is no ordinary executive. Having co-founded Nvidia at 30, he built it into a company worth [$5.8 trillion](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/nvidia-stock-huang-ai-sp500-markets.html) at its peak.

But even as he cultivated a rock star persona in the tech world, [leather jackets and all](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/style/jensen-huang-nvidia-leather-jacket-ai.html), Mr. Huang often evoked his humble beginnings at Denny’s.

He has said that at 15, he got his first job at a Denny’s in Oregon, where his family lived after immigrating from Taiwan. On Thursday, his LinkedIn profile listed two jobs: founder and chief executive of Nvidia (1993-present) and “dishwasher, busboy, waiter” at Denny’s (1978-1983).

“I was a dishwasher, I was a busboy, I waited tables,” Mr. Huang said, according to a [Nvidia blog post in 2023](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-dennys-trillion/) about the unveiling of the plaque. “No one can carry more coffee cups than I can.”

Denny’s has hundreds of locations across the United States, including eight in San Jose, Calif., in the heart of Silicon Valley. The chain’s slogan, “America’s diner is always open,” is meant literally — Denny’s really is open all day, every day, Thanksgiving and Christmas included — but also as a way to showcase the chain’s philosophy.

“We’re open to whomever you are, and we greet customers with open arms and have an open mind,” Peter McGuinness, the chief executive of the agency behind the slogan, [told The New York Times in 2011](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/02/business/media/02adco.html).

For a corporate titan looking to shake off sex scandals and the whiff of espionage, that is a welcome message.

James Paton contributed reporting.
